text: Not sure why we wouldn't want to discuss the ideas of a prominent technologist like Elon here. I know a lot of people disagree with his politics, but it's hard to discuss technology without mentioning him. What Elon says in that clip does seem to be a likely outcome if you take the bitter lesson to its conclusion. As for consumerism if Elons optimistic predictions come to pass we will probably think of a lot of goods similarly to how we think of air today. The bigger question I think is how it will affect producers. If we hit post-scarcity will some of us still need to find a purpose, and what will it be?

text:
I know some real Musk fans: people who've worked with him and like it.  However, he is the kind of person who does not know the limits of his competency, so it's hard to know whether a given comment is worth paying attention to.  And Rogan as interviewer is the not the least bit critical.  So that should help explain why even a minute long quote like this would not be deemed worthy of attention.

On to the substance though: I'm really interested in the idea of AI used for bespoke interfaces.  And one thing I've learned is that you want a means by which a one-off answer/process that the AI thought hard to give becomes automated. codified. and standardized.  Not for efficiency sake, but for predictability.  You want to know that the view is a "simple," reproducible function of the underlying data.

text:
<@UD4Q9LT52>
> If we hit post-scarcity
We won't. That's the other problem with people like Elon Musk (in addition to being a bad person): hubris. If you listen to anyone who has made a serious effort to understand stocks and flows of resources in our universe, you will find out that this dream of post-scarcity will never come true, unless there are very serious and resource-relevant holes in our understanding of physics.
Well, there is one exception: a drastic reduction of the human population of this planet. The survivors can enjoy post-scarcity for a while. At a poverty level, but still.

text:
*Musks Depressing Philosophers*
• #tags: #elon_musk #philosophy #nietzsche
• 
• EM: "We happened to have some books by Nietzsche and Schopenhauer in the house, which you should not read at age 14"
• 
• EM: "I guess when I was around 12 or 15…I had an existential crisis, and I was reading various books on trying to figure out the meaning of life and what does it all mean? It all seemed quite meaningless and then we happened to have some books by Nietzsche and Schopenhauer in the house, which you should not read at age 14 (laughter). It is bad, it’s really negative. So then I read Hitchhikers Guide to the Galaxy which is quite positive I think and it highlighted an important point which is that a lot of times the question is harder than the answer. And if you can properly phrase the question, then the answer is the easy part. So, to the degree that we can better understand the universe, then we can better know what questions to ask. Then whatever the question is that most approximates: what’s the meaning of life? That’s the question we can ultimately get closer to understanding. And so I thought to the degree that we can expand the scope and scale of consciousness and knowledge, then that would be a good thing." Source: <https://www.freshdialogues.com/2013/02/07/transcript-of-elon-musk-interview-with-alison-van-diggelen-iron-man-growing-up-in-south-africa/>
•
